transcript.text: Tax Wedges and Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-02
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate tax wedges, buyer and seller prices, quantity effects, and revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A per-unit tax creates a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. The wedge reduces the quantity traded because some exchanges whose benefits formerly exceeded their costs no longer occur. Tax revenue equals the per-unit wedge multiplied by the post-tax quantity, while the lost mutually beneficial trades create deadweight loss.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify the tax wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive.
Use the post-tax quantity, not the original equilibrium quantity, when measuring revenue.
Tax revenue equals the per-unit tax multiplied by the quantity traded after the tax.
A tax normally reduces quantity traded and creates deadweight loss from forgone exchanges.
WATCH OUT
Tax revenue equals the per-unit tax times the quantity actually traded after the tax. Use the $6 wedge and 80 units here; do not multiply by the original untaxed quantity.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING TAX REVENUE

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price in dollars. Demand slopes down. Supply slopes up, intersecting demand at quantity 100 and price 15. A parallel Supply + tax curve above supply intersects demand at quantity 80 and price 18. At quantity 80, original supply is at price 12. Dashed guides also mark prices 10 and 20 and quantities 65, 120 and 150.

The untaxed equilibrium is $15 at 100 units. After the tax, buyers pay $18, sellers receive $12, and quantity falls to 80. The tax wedge is $18 - $12 = $6 per unit, so government revenue is $6 x 80 = $480.
CHECK YOURSELF
Buyers pay $18 after a tax and sellers receive $12. What is the tax per unit?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Elasticity and Total Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-08
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Connect Elasticity and Total Revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity, and the effect of a price change depends on demand elasticity. A point on demand supplies the price and quantity needed to calculate revenue. At unit elasticity the price and quantity percentage effects offset, marking the revenue peak on a standard linear demand curve.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Calculate total revenue as price multiplied by quantity at each relevant point.
If price and total revenue move in opposite directions, demand is elastic over that range.
If price and total revenue move in the same direction, demand is inelastic over that range.
At unit elasticity, a small price change leaves total revenue approximately unchanged.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to compute elasticity without checking the associated total-revenue change. With elastic demand, price and total revenue move in opposite directions; with inelastic demand, they move together.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ELASTICITY AND REVENUE

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. A straight downward-sloping Demand line runs from price 16 at quantity 0 to price 0 at quantity 120. Its marked points are C at quantity 30, price 12; B at quantity 60, price 8; and A at quantity 90, price 4. Dashed guides show each point on both axes.

At point C, price is $12 and quantity is 30, so total revenue is $12 x 30 = $360. At point B, price is $8 and quantity is 60, so revenue is $480. Moving from C to B lowers price but raises total revenue by $120, indicating elastic demand over that segment.
CHECK YOURSELF

Cruise-cabin price falls from $3,200 to $2,880 while quantity rises from 1,500 to 1,900. Calculate midpoint elasticity and both revenue totals. Is demand elastic over this range, and does revenue rise or fall?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-11
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Producer surplus is the difference between the price a seller receives and the seller's willingness to accept. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Producer surplus is the price-cost gap across units supplied. Producer surplus measures the price received above the seller’s willingness to accept for that unit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a seller's willingness to accept or marginal cost and the price received.
Individual producer surplus equals price received minus willingness to accept.
On a graph, producer surplus is the area above supply and below the market price up to the quantity traded.
A seller whose cost exceeds the market price does not make that trade.
WATCH OUT
Producer surplus is the price received minus willingness to accept, summed over units sold. Do not confuse this per-unit price-cost gap with total revenue.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING PRODUCER SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.
At equilibrium, price is $14 and quantity is 8. The supply intercept is $6, so producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why is the full area above supply not producer surplus?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-12
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Total surplus equals consumer surplus plus producer surplus and measures the gains created by exchange. Each trade adds to total surplus when the buyer's willingness to pay exceeds the seller's opportunity cost. Total surplus is maximized when every mutually beneficial trade occurs and no trade with a cost above its value is completed.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Add consumer surplus and producer surplus to obtain total surplus.
For each possible trade, compare the buyer's willingness to pay with the seller's opportunity cost.
A trade creates gains when buyer value exceeds seller cost.
On a graph, total surplus is the area between demand and supply up to the quantity traded.
WATCH OUT
Total surplus adds consumer and producer surplus. A payment between buyers and sellers changes its distribution; a trade whose cost exceeds buyer value reduces total surplus.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING TOTAL SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.
The graph's equilibrium is 8 units at $14. Consumer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($30 - $14) = $64, and producer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32. Total surplus is therefore $64 + $32 = $96.
CHECK YOURSELF
Buyer value is $17 and seller cost is $22. Efficient action?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Efficient Quantity & Allocation
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-13
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify Efficient Quantity & Allocation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The efficient quantity includes every unit whose buyer value is at least as large as its opportunity cost. Efficiency pairs the highest-value buyers with the lowest-cost sellers and continues exchange while the next buyer's willingness to pay covers the next seller's cost. Producing beyond that point destroys surplus, while stopping before it leaves gains unrealized.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Order potential trades from the highest buyer value and the lowest seller cost.
Complete every trade for which willingness to pay is at least as large as opportunity cost.
Stop when the next seller's cost exceeds the next buyer's value.
An efficient allocation sends the good to the highest-value buyers and production to the lowest-cost sellers.
WATCH OUT
More output is not always more efficient. Stop when the next unit costs more to produce than its buyer is willing to pay.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING THE EFFICIENT QUANTITY

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 18 at quantity 0 and reaches price 2 at quantity 16. Upward-sloping S starts at price 2 and reaches price 18 at quantity 16. They intersect at E, quantity 8 and price 10, with dashed guides to the axes. Demand lies above supply to the left of E and below supply to its right.

Demand and supply intersect at 8 units and $10. At that quantity, the marginal buyer's value equals the marginal seller's cost. Units below 8 create positive gains from trade; units above 8 cost more than buyers value them. The efficient allocation therefore produces 8 units.
CHECK YOURSELF

Five buyers value one pass each at $27, $23, $18, $13, and $8. Five sellers have costs of $4, $10, $15, $21, and $25. How many trades create nonnegative gains, and why should the next trade not occur?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-16
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine Domestic Production, Consumption & Trade Quantities.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

At a world price, domestic consumption is read from demand and domestic production is read from supply. When domestic consumption exceeds domestic production, imports fill the difference; when production exceeds consumption, the excess is exported. The comparison must be made at the world price because that price guides both domestic buyers and sellers under free trade.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare the world price with the domestic no-trade equilibrium price.
At the world price, read domestic consumption from demand and domestic production from supply.
When consumption exceeds production, imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production.
When production exceeds consumption, exports equal domestic production minus domestic consumption.
WATCH OUT

When the world price exceeds the domestic no-trade equilibrium price, domestic supply exceeds domestic demand. The difference is exports, not imports. Do not infer tariff revenue or deadweight loss from this free-trade example.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING EXPORTS

Horizontal axis: quantity of avocados in thousands; vertical axis: price of avocados in dollars. Domestic demand slopes down and domestic supply slopes up. They intersect at A, quantity 175 thousand and price 7. A horizontal world-price line marked Pw = $10 meets demand at 100 thousand and supply at 250 thousand. Dashed vertical guides show those quantities.

Without trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at $7 and 175 thousand avocados. At the $10 world price, domestic consumers buy 100 thousand while domestic producers supply 250 thousand. The country exports the difference: 250 - 100 = 150 thousand avocados.
CHECK YOURSELF
Using the avocado export-market graph, what are domestic production, domestic consumption, and exports at Pw=$10?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-22
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Average fixed cost, average variable cost, and average total cost express costs per unit of output. Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost. Average fixed cost falls as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units, while average variable cost changes with the productivity and price of variable inputs.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Divide fixed cost by output for average fixed cost and variable cost by output for average variable cost.
Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost.
Average fixed cost falls continuously as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units.
Use per-unit measures only when output is positive.
WATCH OUT
Average costs are per unit; total costs are not. Subtract AVC from ATC to find AFC, then multiply AFC by positive output to recover total fixed cost.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING AVERAGE-COST CURVES

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: costs in dollars. Curves are labeled MC, AC and AVC. MC first dips slightly and then rises. It crosses AVC at its minimum, quantity 200 and cost 10. At quantity 400, MC crosses AC at its minimum of 20, while AVC is 12. Dashed guides mark the quantities and costs. AC remains above AVC.

At 400 units, the graph shows average cost of $20 and average variable cost of $12. Because AC = AVC + AFC, average fixed cost is $20 - $12 = $8 per unit. The gap between AC and AVC is therefore the firm's average fixed cost.
CHECK YOURSELF
At Q = 30, AVC is $14 and ATC is $24. Calculate AFC and total fixed cost. Verify your answer by multiplying the per-unit gap by output.
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-32
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze Short-Run Supply & Cost Shifts.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A competitive firm's short-run supply curve is the rising portion of marginal cost at and above minimum average variable cost. The tax is tied to each unit produced. MC gives the additional cost of supply. The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use the rising portion of marginal cost at and above minimum average variable cost as firm supply.
A variable-input cost increase shifts marginal cost and short-run supply upward or left.
A fixed-cost change shifts average total cost but leaves marginal cost and short-run supply unchanged.
Distinguish a movement along supply caused by price from a shift caused by production conditions.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume fixed cost shifts supply. The short-run supply schedule depends on marginal and variable costs, not fixed cost. Fixed cost affects profit but not the short-run MC-above-AVC supply schedule.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING SHORT-RUN FIRM SUPPLY

Horizontal axis: firm quantity; vertical axis: cost / revenue. Horizontal P = MR = AR is at 10, below the entire AVC curve. MC crosses minimum AVC at A, quantity 22 and cost 20. Other marked points on rising MC are B near quantity 36 and cost 30, C near quantity 44 and cost 41 at minimum ATC, and D near quantity 50 and cost 50. Unprinted coordinates are approximate. ATC is above AVC.

The firm's short-run supply curve is the portion of MC at and above minimum AVC, which begins at point A: 22 units and $20. For example, if market price rises to $30, the firm supplies the quantity at point B, about 36 units. MC below A is not part of supply because the firm shuts down.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which MC segment is competitive short-run supply?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-33
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace entry, exit, zero economic profit, normal profit, and long-run competitive adjustment.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Entry and exit move a competitive industry toward long-run equilibrium with zero economic profit. More firms supply more total output at each price. At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit. Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit.
Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.
Long-run industry assessment 10: Demand falls in a constant-cost industry and some firms leave.
Long-run industry assessment 11: Demand rises in a constant-cost industry and entry is unrestricted.
WATCH OUT

Do not miss long run equilibrium conditions. At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit. Entry and exit remove persistent economic profit or loss in the benchmark model.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ENTRY AND ZERO ECONOMIC PROFIT

Two panels. Left, Market: horizontal axis market quantity; vertical axis price. S slopes up and D slopes down, intersecting at quantity 100 and price 25. Right, Representative firm: horizontal axis firm quantity; vertical axis cost / revenue. Horizontal P = MR = AR at 25 meets MC and minimum ATC at quantity 50. At that quantity, AVC is 17, explicitly labeled and connected by dashed guides. ATC and AVC are U-shaped. Both panels share price 25.

If firms initially earn economic profit, entry expands market supply and pushes price down. If they incur losses, exit reduces supply and pushes price up. The graph shows the endpoint: P = MC, and price equals minimum ATC at $25 and 50 units. Revenue covers explicit and implicit costs, so no entry or exit pressure remains.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why can accounting profit be positive at zero economic profit?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.

transcript.text: Profit-Maximizing Output & Monopoly Price
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-38
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Apply Profit-Maximizing Output & Monopoly Price.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A monopolist compares marginal revenue with marginal cost to choose output, then reads the corresponding price from demand. In the displayed interior solution, MR exceeds MC before their crossing and falls below MC afterward. The output decision and the price decision are separate; marginal cost need not always slope upward.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Find the output where MR crosses MC from above in the interior solution.
Move vertically from that output to the demand curve to find the monopoly price.
Keep the output decision and price decision separate: marginal conditions determine quantity, demand determines price.
Do not set price equal to marginal revenue or marginal cost unless the graph happens to imply it.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to read monopoly price from the marginal-revenue curve. Find output where MR = MC, then read the price buyers will pay from demand.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING MONOPOLY PRICE

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D slopes down from price 60 at quantity 0 to zero at 120. MR slopes down more steeply, reaching zero at 60. At quantity 40, MR and rising MC meet at 20; demand is at 40 and ATC at 45, with dashed guides. Demand and MC intersect near quantity 67 and price 27. ATC is U-shaped, reaching its minimum to the right of quantity 40. The 67 and 27 intersection values are approximate as labeled.

The monopolist first finds output where MR = MC, which occurs at 40 units and a marginal value of $20. It then moves up to the demand curve, where buyers will pay $40 for 40 units. The profit-maximizing choice is therefore Q = 40 and P = $40, not the $20 MR value.
CHECK YOURSELF
What is the correct order for solving a monopoly graph?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Monopoly Welfare, Efficiency & Competitive Comparison
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-40
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Compare Monopoly Welfare, Efficiency & Competitive Comparison.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Compared with competition, monopoly usually restricts output, raises price, transfers surplus, and creates deadweight loss. Transfers remain in total surplus; unrealized trades do not. The omitted units would generate positive gains from trade. Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare monopoly output and price with the competitive benchmark where price equals marginal cost.
Monopoly normally produces less and charges more than a competitive market.
Separate the transfer of surplus to the monopolist from surplus lost through reduced output.
Deadweight loss is the value of trades between monopoly output and the efficient quantity that no longer occur.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to reverse monopoly competitive comparison. Market power generally leads the monopolist to restrict output and charge a higher price than the competitive benchmark.
WORKED EXAMPLE: IDENTIFYING MONOPOLY DEADWEIGHT LOSS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D slopes down, and MR slopes down more steeply from the same vertical intercept. MC is horizontal at 20. MR meets MC near quantity 45; at that quantity, guides mark demand price about 47 and ATC about 24. Demand meets MC at quantity 90 and price 20; ATC there is slightly above 20. ATC declines throughout the displayed relevant range. The marked demand price at 45 is approximately 47.

The unregulated monopoly chooses about 45 units where MR = MC and charges the demand price of about $47. The efficient outcome occurs where demand meets MC: 90 units at $20. Monopoly therefore restricts output and raises price, leaving mutually beneficial units between 45 and 90 unproduced.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which part of lost consumer surplus is deadweight loss?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-44
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Short-Run Firm Choice, Profit/Loss & Shutdown uses MR = MC, firm demand, ATC, and AVC to determine output, price, profit or loss, and short-run shutdown. The firm shuts down when price cannot cover variable cost. At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Use marginal revenue and rising marginal cost to choose the firm's output.
Read price and average total cost at that output to determine profit or loss.
Use average variable cost to determine whether the firm operates or shuts down in the short run.
Keep output choice, profit measurement, and shutdown analysis as three distinct steps.
WATCH OUT
Separate profit from shutdown. A fixed-cost increase can create an economic loss without changing marginal cost or the benefit of operating; compare revenue with variable cost.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHORT-RUN FIRM DECISION

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D = AR slopes down; MR slopes down more steeply and reaches zero at quantity 60. At marked quantity 36, MR and MC meet at 15, while demand and ATC meet at 27. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those values. ATC continues downward to a minimum near quantity 50 before rising; MC rises to the right of 36.

The displayed baseline has Q = 36 and P = ATC = $27, so economic profit is zero. Consider a higher fixed lease cost of $108, with demand and variable costs unchanged. Output and price stay at that baseline, but ATC rises by $3 and the loss is $108. The firm still operates if revenue covers variable cost; loss alone does not imply shutdown.
CHECK YOURSELF
A firm earns a loss because P is below ATC. What additional cost comparison is needed to decide whether it should shut down in the short run?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-45
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace Entry, Exit & Long-Run Equilibrium.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

In monopolistic competition, short-run profit attracts entry and short-run loss causes exit until economic profit is zero. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Excess capacity compares equilibrium Q with minimum-ATC Q.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Short-run economic profit attracts entry, which reduces each incumbent firm's demand.
Short-run losses cause exit, which raises the demand facing surviving firms.
Long-run equilibrium occurs when the firm's demand is tangent to average total cost and economic profit is zero.
Distinguish zero economic profit from zero accounting profit.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to equate zero economic and accounting profit. Entry and exit remove economic profit in both models. Zero economic profit is an entry condition, not proof of allocative or productive efficiency.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ENTRY, EXIT, AND LONG-RUN PROFIT

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price / cost. Demand D = AR slopes down; MR slopes down more steeply and reaches zero at quantity 60. At marked quantity 36, MR and MC meet at 15, while demand and ATC meet at 27. Dashed horizontal and vertical guides mark those values. ATC continues downward to a minimum near quantity 50 before rising; MC rises to the right of 36.

Short-run profit attracts competing varieties, reducing demand for each incumbent. Adjustment continues until demand is tangent to ATC at the chosen output. The graph shows that endpoint at 36 units and $27, where revenue and cost both equal $972. Tangency eliminates economic profit; it does not put output at minimum ATC.
CHECK YOURSELF
What does excess capacity measure?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-48
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify Oligopoly Structure, Strategic Interdependence & Concentration.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

An oligopoly contains only a few important firms, so each firm's decisions depend on expected rival responses. Differentiation can exist in both; strategic few-firm response is distinctive. Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly. With only a few important firms, one firm’s action can provoke responses that change its own payoff.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a market dominated by a few firms with meaningful barriers to entry.
Each firm's price, output, or advertising decision depends on how rivals are expected to respond.
Use concentration measures as evidence about structure, not as a complete verdict about competition.
The defining clue is strategic interdependence among the important firms.
WATCH OUT
Do not use firm count alone. Dominant shares and strategic interdependence point to oligopoly. Concentration depends on the boundaries of the relevant market.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MEASURING MARKET CONCENTRATION

Horizontal axis: Firm or fringe, with categories A, B, C, D and Other; vertical axis: Market share in percent. The five bars have printed values A 38 percent, B 32 percent, C 12 percent, D 9 percent, and Other 9 percent. Other is a separate aggregate category, not labeled as a single firm.

The named firms contribute 38^2 + 32^2 + 12^2 + 9^2 = 2,693 HHI points. The remaining 9% is labeled Other, an unspecified fringe. If it were one firm, it would add 9^2 = 81 points. Thus 2,774 is an upper bound, not an exact HHI. An exact calculation requires the individual fringe shares.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why can an aggregate Other category not generally be squared as if it were one firm when calculating exact HHI?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Dynamic Strategy: Repeated Games, Credibility & Entry Deterrence
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-51
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze repeated games, credible commitments, entry deterrence, and sequential strategic choices.
Difficulty: Advanced
THE CORE IDEA

In a sequential game, one player acts before another. Work backward from the last decision: identify the action that the later player will actually prefer, then use that response to evaluate the first move. A threat is credible only if carrying it out would be worthwhile when the decision arrives. Repeated interaction can make future consequences matter, but no present-value calculation is needed here.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Determine whether firms interact once or expect to meet again.
Compare the immediate gain from cheating or entering with future losses from retaliation.
A threat affects behavior only when carrying it out would be credible.
Longer relationships, patience, and observable actions make cooperative outcomes easier to sustain.
WATCH OUT
A threatened response is not automatically credible. Compare the later player's payoffs at the decision point before using the threat to predict the first move.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TESTING A CREDIBLE THREAT

Sequential game tree; payoffs are ordered Entrant, Incumbent. The Entrant moves first. Stay out ends with payoffs (0, 12). Enter leads to the Incumbent decision node. From that node, Accommodate ends with (6, 7), and Fight ends with (negative 3, 3). Branch labels identify the actions; each payoff belongs to its branch endpoint.

The game tree is solved backward. If entry occurs, the incumbent receives 7 by accommodating and 3 by fighting, so accommodation is the credible response on that branch. Anticipating it, the entrant compares 6 from entering with 0 from staying out and enters. The backward-induction outcome is Enter, then Accommodate.
CHECK YOURSELF
After entry, why will the incumbent accommodate rather than fight, and how does that affect the entrant's first decision?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Factor Markets & Labor Demand
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-57
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use marginal productivity to analyze labor demand, wages, and employment.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Labor demand is derived from the value workers add to output. Marginal product of labor is the extra output from one more worker. For a price-taking seller, VMP = output price x MPL. A profit-maximizing firm hires labor up to the point where VMP equals the wage.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A wage change causes movement along labor demand; productivity or output-price changes shift labor demand.
Higher product demand, output price, or worker productivity shifts labor demand right.
Worker preferences, population, migration, training, and alternative jobs can shift labor supply.
Competitive wage and employment occur where market labor demand intersects market labor supply.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse MPL with VMP. MPL is extra physical output; VMP converts that output into dollars by multiplying by the output price.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMPETITIVE LABOR-MARKET EQUILIBRIUM

Horizontal axis: hundreds of warehouse workers; vertical axis: hourly wage in dollars. Labor Demand slopes down from wage 30 at quantity 0 to zero at 120 hundreds. Labor Supply slopes up from wage 10. They intersect at wage 20 and quantity 40 hundreds of workers, with dashed guides to both axes. Supply lies above demand to the right of that intersection.

Suppose output sells for $5 and the marginal worker adds 4 units per hour. VMP is $5 x 4 = $20 per hour, matching a $20 wage. The graph shows market equilibrium at that wage and 40 hundreds of workers, or 4,000 workers. A higher output price raises VMP at each employment level and shifts labor demand right.
CHECK YOURSELF
If the output price rises while worker productivity is unchanged, what happens to labor demand?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Consumer Choice
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-58
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use a budget constraint and preferences to identify the best affordable bundle.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A budget constraint shows affordable bundles at given income and prices. Its intercepts show the most of either good a consumer can buy. An indifference curve connects bundles the consumer ranks equally. The best affordable bundle reaches the highest available preference level; in this example, its curve just touches the budget line.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Bundles inside or on the budget line are feasible; bundles outside it are infeasible.
An income change shifts the line in parallel when prices are fixed.
A change in one price pivots the line around the unchanged intercept.
Compare the highest preference curve that can be reached without exceeding the budget.
WATCH OUT
Spending the whole budget is not enough to prove optimality. The chosen bundle must also provide the highest attainable preference ranking.
WORKED EXAMPLE: BEST AFFORDABLE BUNDLE

Horizontal axis: Good X; vertical axis: Good Y. A straight budget line runs from 40 units of Y at X = 0 to 20 units of X at Y = 0. Marked bundle A is X = 10 and Y = 20. At A the budget line is tangent to solid IC2. Dashed IC1 lies below IC2 and intersects the feasible set; dashed IC3 lies above IC2 and outside the budget line. All three indifference curves slope down and are convex toward the origin.

The budget line reaches 20 units of X or 40 units of Y, so its slope is -2. Bundle A contains 10 units of X and 20 of Y. At A, the budget line is tangent to IC2, the highest attainable indifference curve. IC3 is preferred but lies outside the feasible set, while IC1 is attainable but provides a lower ranking.
CHECK YOURSELF
If only the price of Y falls, does the budget line shift in parallel or pivot?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
